title: this Binding
subtitle: Call-site rules vs lexical this in arrows

cards.front: Is this looked up like a normal variable?
cards.meaning: No — except for arrow functions, which have no this binding of their own. For ordinary functions, this is decided mostly by how the function is called (the call site), plus hard overrides: new, bind, and arrows.

cards.front: Variables vs this — one sentence each?
cards.meaning: Variable lookup is lexical (where code was written). For ordinary functions, this is decided mostly by how the function is called (call site), plus new, bind, and arrows (lexical this).

cards.front: Call-site checklist for this (ordinary vs arrow)?
cards.meaning: Ask: (1) called with new? (2) call/apply, or a function from bind? (3) something.fn(...)? (4) otherwise bare call → default binding. (5) If the function is an arrow, skip 1–4 for this: use the enclosing scope’s this. That ordering is the precedence list.
Highest to lowest: new binding, explicit (call/apply/bind), implicit (obj.method()), default (bare fn()). Arrows ignore this ladder — use enclosing lexical this.
undefined in strict mode; the global object in sloppy mode.
obj. Implicit binding: the object left of the final property access is the receiver.
x. Explicit binding sets this (and optionally arguments) yourself.
x, permanently for that bound function.
The newly created instance (unless the constructor returns another object).
Whatever this was in the enclosing lexical scope. Call-site rules 1–4 do not apply.

cards.front: Bare fn() — this in strict vs sloppy?
cards.meaning: Strict (modules, class bodies, 'use strict'): undefined. Sloppy: global object (globalThis). Modern React/TS/ESM → expect undefined on detached calls.
cards.example: 'use strict'; function f() { return this; } f(); // undefined

cards.meaning: Default binding — not obj.read(). Implicit binding needs call shape receiver.method(); a bare function reference loses the receiver.
cards.notes: strict: TypeError reading property of undefined.

cards.meaning: Default binding. The timer later does a bare call, not obj.method(), so implicit binding never applies. Same family as passing this.handleClick as a callback.
The object immediately left of the final call — here obj.nested, not obj. Only the last link before () is the receiver.
Methods need a convenient reference to “the object I was invoked on” without passing that object as an argument every time.
Anything that separates the function from the call’s receiver: const greet = a.b.greet; greet(); setTimeout(a.b.greet, 0); const { greet: g } = a.b; g(); All become default binding.

Without thisArg, this is not user (forEach may set its own thisArg; without it, default / undefined in strict). With thisArg user, explicit thisArg is OK. Wrapping [1].forEach(() => user.print()) keeps the call shape user.print().
call: invoke immediately with listed args. apply: invoke immediately with args as an array (or array-like). bind: return a new function permanently tied to thisArg (and optional partial args).
call → 'Hi, Nika'. apply(person, ['Hi']) → 'Hi, Nika'. bind(person) then bound('Hey') → 'Hey, Nika'.

Returns a new function permanently tied to thisArg for later bare calls (e.g. setTimeout). bind does not mutate the original function. Bound this sticks — later call/apply won't rebind as beginners expect.
cards.example: const stable = obj.read.bind(obj); setTimeout(stable, 0); // this === obj

cards.front: call/apply on an already-bound function — new this?
cards.meaning: Not the way beginners expect. Bound functions ignore later implicit/default calls, and call/apply do not re-bind this to a new target — the bound this sticks.

cards.front: call/apply with thisArg null or undefined?
cards.meaning: Strict mode: this is actually that value (null or undefined). Sloppy mode: they coerce to the global object.
15. bind creates a new exotic function; useful for partial application as well as this.
cards.example: function add(a, b) { return a + b; } const add10 = add.bind(null, 10); add10(5); // 15

cards.front: What does new Fn(...args) roughly do?
cards.meaning: (1) Create a new ordinary object. (2) Set that object’s prototype link from Fn.prototype. (3) Call Fn with this bound to the new object. (4) If the constructor returns an object, that object is the result; otherwise use the new object.
cards.example: function User(name) { this.name = name; } const u = new User('Ada'); u.name; // 'Ada'

cards.front: new Bound() when F was bound to obj?
cards.meaning: new wins over bind's thisArg for construction — this is the new instance, not obj. new has highest precedence among ordinary call-site rules.
cards.example: const Bound = F.bind(obj); const x = new Bound(); x.tag; // 'instance'

cards.meaning: Default this — pollutes global, or throws in strict when assigning this.name. That is why constructors are capitalized by convention and why classes force new.

cards.front: Do arrow functions get this from the four call-site rules?
cards.meaning: No. They have no own this binding. Evaluating this inside an arrow resolves like a variable in the enclosing lexical scope (the this that the outer non-arrow context would see — or the outer arrow’s inherited this, and so on).
Not the object. Object literals don't create a this binding for the arrow; it captures lexical this from outside (often undefined in modules), not implicit obj.
cards.example: obj.regular(); // this=obj. obj.arrow(); // lexical, typically undefined name.

cards.meaning: Default binding — undefined in strict / TypeError on property access. regular used implicit binding only when called as obj.regular().
cards.example:
obj.regular(); // 'nika'
const detached = obj.regular; detached(); // default

cards.front: Why arrow in setTimeout inside start() fixes this.ms?
cards.meaning: Arrow has no own this; it uses this from enclosing start() where implicit binding made this the timer object. Regular function callback gets default binding, not timer2.
cards.example:
timer.start(); // arrow logs this.ms from timer
setTimeout(function () { console.log(this.ms); } // default, not timer2

cards.front: What else do arrows lack besides own this?
cards.meaning: No own arguments; cannot be used as constructors (new arrow → TypeError); no own super binding in the same way methods do. For this interviews, the headline is: lexical this, call site ignored.
TypeError. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors.
Created per instance where this is the instance, so the arrow lexically captures that instance — stable this when passed as detached handler (React class pattern).
Both true for a non-arrow f. obj.f() is implicit; f.call(obj) is explicit.
cards.example:
const obj = { f }; obj.f() === obj; // true
f.call(obj) === obj; // true

cards.meaning: obj if f was called as obj.f() — the arrow captured this from f's implicit binding at the call that created it.
cards.example: const obj = { f() { return () => this; } }; const arrow = obj.f(); arrow(); // obj

cards.meaning: React invokes a bare function reference, not component.handleClick(), so implicit binding never applies; class bodies are strict → this is undefined → this.props throws.
cards.notes: Fix: constructor bind, class field arrow, or inline () => this.handleClick().

cards.front: React class handler bug — five mechanism steps?
cards.meaning: (1) this.handleClick evaluates to a function reference. (2) React stores and later invokes it as a bare callback. (3) Implicit binding requires receiver.method(). (4) Class bodies are strict → default this is undefined. (5) Reading this.props throws.

cards.front: Three fixes for the React class this.handleClick bug?
cards.meaning: (1) Constructor bind: this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this). (2) Class field arrow: handleClick = () => { ... } (lexical this). (3) Inline arrow in render: onClick={() => this.handleClick()} — call shape restores implicit binding (new function each render; sometimes relevant for memoization/perf). Function components sidestep this because there's no this.
cards.notes: Modern codebases often avoid the issue with function components.

cards.meaning: this.handleClick is passed as a bare reference to onClick — React calls it as a plain function, not as this.handleClick(), so the implicit binding rule never applies and this falls back to undefined in strict mode (all ES modules and class bodies are strict by default). Three fixes: bind in the constructor; use a class field arrow which lexically captures this; or pass an inline arrow at the call site. Function components sidestep this because there's no this to bind.
Default binding — destructuring extracts the function without the receiver; call is greet(), not a.b.greet().

cards.front: Does this mean the function’s enclosing object in the source?
cards.meaning: For ordinary functions, no — look at the call. Object-literal arrows do not get that object as this either; they bind lexically to the enclosing scope’s this, which may be undefined in modules.

cards.front: Do arrows bind this to the object they are defined on?
cards.meaning: No. They bind lexically to the enclosing scope’s this, which may be undefined in modules — not “the object they are defined on.”

Closures capture variables lexically. Ordinary this is not a variable lookup (arrows make this behave like lexical capture). Closures answer which variable binding; this answers which receiver object for non-arrows. Mixing the two explanations is a common interview failure.

cards.front: Does bind mutate the original function?
cards.meaning: No. It returns a new function.

cards.front: Use arrows as prototype methods that need dynamic this?
cards.meaning: Avoid that. If you need per-call receivers (e.g. borrowing methods), use regular functions.

cards.front: Bare calls in modern React/TS/ESM — this is window?
cards.meaning: No. Forgetful sloppy-mode thinking. Bare calls in modern React/TS/ESM are undefined, not window. Class bodies and modules are strict.
